text_fidelity_a:
Toysmith Euler's Disk This works ok.  The disc is metal and very heavy.  But the plastic base for the mirror is far too flimsy and lightweight to accommodate the disc without a lot of flexing and popping and clapping noise.  All of this  means lost energy which reduces spin time.  The product just doesn't implement well the design the patent describes.

I wanted to better stabilize the base, so under running hot water I very carefully removed the mirror from the base.  Perhaps not something I would recommend.  As I was doing so, the smell of whatever adhesive was used literally made me light-headed.  I've used a lot of epoxies and adhesives, but none that smelled as strong as this, like really strong gasoline.  The adhesive was soft and spongy, not fully cured.  I carefully removed all of  whatever it was and filled the gap between the base and the bottom of the mirror with air-dry clay to fill the gaps and to increase the weight of the base overall.  It did help to increase spin time somewhat and got rid of the annoying galloping-horse-playing-steel-drum sounds.
text_fidelity_b: Toysmith Euler's Disk

text_fidelity_a: Creativity for Kids Beaded Snowflake Ornaments - Create 6 Christmas Tree Ornaments Eh. Was a lot more work than you would think and NOT much fun.  I did end up making them, but one of the wire forms broke - so only ended up with 5. Definitely set up with towel under your work area because you WILL drop the beads and forms as you're working on them and after about 20 times picking up everything up off the floor, you'll want to figure out a way to keep the beads on a non-floor surface.  They do come with envelopes and seals if you intend to gift them.  Oh, and they include a tiny tube of glue to put on the rubber tips - you will NEED to do this on ALL the tips if you want them to stay on.  Another think I noticed is that if I would have 6 finished, I would have been short 4 rubber tips - which would have rendered the last snowflake - garbage.  If you can't tip the ends, the beads don't stay on. So, the rubber tips are SUPER important.  There were plenty of beads to stretch your artistic wings.  But count your rubber tips first so you will know how many you can actually make.  Eh.  I would not recommend this kit based on the missing pieces and the broken wire of one snowflake.  I did not rate on my dislike of the task.

LEGO Disney Frozen Elsa's Magical Ice Palace 43172 Toy Castle Building Kit with Mini Dolls, Castle Playset with Popular Frozen Characters Including Elsa, Olaf, Anna and More (701 Pieces) I’m a lover of the really big LEGO sets, especially the Creator buildings (e.g., Cinderella’s Castle; the Detective’s Office) and the Technic heavy construction equipment models (e.g., the Bucket Wheel Excavator). In my opinion, this medium-sized set, the DISNEY FROZEN ELSA’S MAGICAL ICE PALACE (41148) is one of LEGO’s very best efforts.

The set has lots of beautiful transparent blue bricks, and a couple of specialized large panels for the castle that are transparent blue with embedded silver sparkles. The transparent blue bricks exactly match Elsa’s blue from the “Frozen” movie.

If you’ve seen the movie, you will love the spiral staircase that expands and rises up with a twist of the ball at the top--very much like the icy castle walls that rose up magically in response to Elsa’s sweeping movements in the movie. As is always true with LEGO sets, it's fun to see, as you build, how the simple bricks become furniture, chandeliers, doorways, and other details.

The set has minifigures of Olaf, Elsa, Anna, a snow monster, and small snowmen. The balconied castle is furnished with a chandelier, a bed with coverlet, a table and chairs, a music stand, and a kitchen. Stickers printed on sparkly silver paper go onto the moving castle doors to complete the dazzling look of the ice palace. And despite all the detail, this set is fairly easy to build.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Disney Frozen Elsa's Magical Ice Palace 43172 Toy Castle Building Kit with Mini Dolls, Castle Playset with Popular Frozen Characters Including Elsa, Olaf, Anna and More (701 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
Drone Home -- First Ever Game With a Real, Flying Drone -- Great, Family Fun! -- For 2-4 Players -- Ages 8+ I have very mixed feelings about this game. First, it is REALLY FUN, and my kids and I were laughing really hard playing it. The drone taking off is really a lot of fun and cool to see, and even our little 3 year old who is too young to play was enamored by it and shrieking when it would lift off with little playing pieces inside! Really a lot of fun.
That being said, there are 3 caveats to be aware of:
1)I don't feel comfortable letting the kids play this alone. The drone comes crashing down sometimes and I want an adult or kid old enough to be able to catch it to avoid hurting anyone / furniture, or crashing so hard it cracks the plastic (a part of the drone siding already popped out, but I was able to push it back into place).

2) I feel like this game won't last very long. The pieces are VERY easily lost, as they end up being flung around the room as you play. Also, the drone lifting off bumps into the ceiling easily (thankfully we have cathedral ceilings in our living and had to move the game over to there, otherwise it would hit and come crashing down fast). It's only a matter of time before the plastic breaks or pieces get lost forever.

3) I dove to catch it on the way down after a particular round, and it hurt my finger. Nothing major, didn't hurt more than stubbing your toe on furniture or stepping on a lego- it has a safety to shut the propeller if it detects something in the way, but I was still surprised. I was fine, but one of my kids would have been crying if it happened to them.

My daughter actually suggested we try playing it outside next time, which might solve some of the issues- can't do damage to the house and everyone can duck for cover until it crashes into the grass. Wind might make it less fun though. HOWEVER- this was a TON OF FUN TO PLAY, so even with all those caveats, and even considering it might not last more than a few months in my household, I'd still consider it worth playing even for those few times. The look on their faces when the drone takes off is PRICELESS, and worth it even if you only get to play it once.

What's nice about that is, if you're anything like me, and you're totally over all types of zombie games, you will still be able to play Hit Z Road.

This game is really a push your luck dice rolling game with auctions. You're trying to survive until the end of the road, and you need to make some meaningful choices along the way that could make your journey much easier, or much more daring. There is some player elimination, but it's not one of those "you can die on the first turn" types of eliminations - our earliest death was about 10 minutes before the end of the game.

I think a lot of people will find the artwork on this game to be fantastic, and I have to admit that it is daring, different, and one of the most unique looking games out there. While I can admire the work that went into it, the art just doesn't appeal to me.

The name, by the way, might be one of the worst in the history of board gaming.

Bgraamiens Puzzle-Blooming Color-1000 Pieces Color Challenge Blue Board Round Jigsaw Puzzles I don’t work on jigsaw puzzles often though I do enjoy them. This is a large puzzle – 1000 pieces – and is a challenge. So far I am pleased with it.

This is a round puzzle, which presents a different kind of challenge than a square or rectangular one, as there are no corners to work from. However, the round edge does provide a starting point in its own right. The pattern and solid non-gradient colors makes this a tough puzzle but it is doable and I am making progress on it. I’m in no hurry but I’m looking forward to seeing the finished puzzle.

I haven’t seen any pieces that are damaged, printed incorrectly or duplicated. I won’t know for sure that none are missing until I’m finished (I’ve seen this issue with another puzzle I worked some time ago), but I have to assume for now that it’s complete.

This is a big, time-consuming puzzle that will take a while to complete. The pattern is pretty, the pieces are made well and the puzzle itself is not unreasonably priced.

text_fidelity_a:
Bright Starts Pop & Giggle Pond Pal Ball Popper Musical Toy, Ages 6 months + This frog is loud and a bit annoying, but it's still cute!

When this toy comes out of the box, you'll have to put together 3 different pieces. The head has to be attached to the body, and a little spring part attaches to the side. There are 6 different colored balls, too.

This toy does NOT come with batteries. You'll need 4 AA batteries, along with a small screwdriver(Phillips head or flat, either one) to get them into the toy.

There are 4 "piano" keys on the front that make sounds, and there's also the main button that will start the music playing and the mouth to bouncing. The inside of the mouth is soft. When the main button is pressed, the inside of the mouth will move around, and make the balls bounce. When the ball hits the center of the mouth, the bouncing will usually cause the ball to bounce outside of the mouth. This is fun for children to then go grabbing the stray balls. If the child is really young, you'll be the one grabbing the balls. (They will go rolling under couches and beds, so try to play it in an area that will result in minimal lost balls.)

Overall, this is a fun toy for young children/babies. The average mama of babies won't want it around too much, though. Between the noise and running after balls, it's a bit exhausting. For mamas of children that are old enough to chase after the balls, it's a great way to burn built up energy on a rainy day! (If playing on carpet, the balls most likely won't roll quite so much.)
text_fidelity_b: Bright Starts Pop & Giggle Pond Pal Ball Popper Musical Toy, Ages 6 months +

Mattel Games Pictionary: Frame Game I was really excited about this product, as Pictionary is one of my all-time favorite party games. This was a disappointment on so many levels.

First, there is no storage box. It comes with a frame, a frame stand, a timer, and a marker. And a dice, which got lost in no time. The "frame" itself is about the size of a sheet of paper (8" by 10"), and it is clear, so you can see through it. The small size makes it ideal for travel or a backpack, but the fact that it is clear makes it difficult to see when holding it on your lap. And forget about using it on the black coffee table. It works much better when used flat, on a light background surface. I like that you can use the frame as a window, so the see-through feature may be useful one at a time. It's pretty much impossible for two people to write on opposite sides of the board at the same time. Honestly it is pretty much for anyone to write on the board when it is in the stand, which keeps the board vertical.

We like to use large dry-erase boards when we pay Pictionary. I would recommend that rather than this game. The frame might be fun to draw on once in a while -- but shy not get a small whiteboard, which is much better suited for the purpose?
text_fidelity_b: Mattel Games Pictionary: Frame Game

text_fidelity_a:
Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games Short version of the review: it’s a fun game with a pretty good first-game learning curve that settles in pretty quickly in subsequent games. It can be long (though you can adjust it). We’ll add it to our rotation of “lengthy” games

Longer version

1) Packing
I’m going to ding the game for packaging because while everything comes fine (as is typical, there’s a lot of popping pieces out of their cardboard sheets), I like when games include easy ways of keeping thing together and/or organized once you’ve played the first game. Even if it’s as minimal as separate small plastic bags. We used our own tiny bags (we’ve learned to keep ones that do come with other games if they’re extra thanks to consolidation) and a few regular small baggies, but I don’t think it’s too much to ask that those things be included

2) Materials
All the materials seem of good quality. Cards are not super-thick but they’re not at all flimsy, the non-plastic pieces feel solid and you don’t have any sense that they’ll start coming apart or getting dented/torn. The plastic cities are a nice touch, but the capital cities could perhaps have been made a little more distinctive. Not at all a big deal; a close look is all you need.

3) Instructions
The big sheet of instructions is fine. Generally clear and well written, with a few “clarification” points at the end, which is a nice touch. We had a few questions that weren’t included, but they were easy to find online. A few individual player cards with a stripped down bit of instruction for quick, easy reference would have been nice to toss in

4) Set up
As noted (and as is usual for these types of games) there’s a lot of popping things out and organizing. Once that’s done the first time, set-up is relatively quick. You put together some map tiles which is easy enough (though this 50+-year-old wouldn’t have minded if the organizing numbers were a little bigger on each tile). Each player gets tokens, a set of cards five of which are laid out in a particular order under their “Focus” bar (the cards are in these areas: Military, Technology, Culture, Economy, Industry), a set of “diplomacy” cards, a “leader” card (who they “play”—Cleopatra for instance), a few caravans (little wagons used for trading). After you’ve done it a few times it’s a pretty quick set-up. You also set up some cards to the side of the play area (World Wonder cards and City-State Diplomacy Cards and Victory Cards (these are what determine how the game is won). This is always an issue in these sorts of game because of course they’re not going to be truly “visible” to all the players. Someone is going to have to move or ask to see them to see what they say (some change throughout the game). I have no idea how to get around that though; it’s just a matter of physical setting.

5) game play
I’m not going to detail it. But generally, the Victory cards have two “agendas” on them, such as build two Wonders of the World, and a player who achieves one agenda from each of the cards is the winner (this is nice because you can shorten the game if desired by simply playing with fewer Victory cards). As far as the play itself
1) Players can “resolve” (do what it says) any one of the five cards below their Focus bar. This might mean building a city, attacking someone, moving a caravan, laying out a “Control” piece to claim a hex space (i.e. territory).
2) Once they’ve done that, that card gets move to slot one under the bar and all the others move one slot to the right. This is key because the slot number affects how the card is resolved. For instance, when you attack using your military card, you roll a die and add the slot number (and possibly other bonuses) to your roll. So you’re going to want to attack when that card is in the 4 or 5 position typically, not the 1 or 2 slot. This adds a nice bit of complexity to your action choices.

That’s pretty much the gameplay for players. A few other factor include
1) You can swap out a card under your focus by advancing your “Tech” counter a certain number (you do that using one of the cards). Once you hit a certain level, you can exchange one low level card for one that’s a bit more powerful. There are 4 levels of cards.
2) Barbarian tokens on the board move at regular periods and they can end up destroying one of your caravans or claiming territory from you (which affects how much money your cities earn and how much you can advance)
3) Caravans allow you to gain trade tokens that can be used to increase the impact of your cards. For example, if you have two trade tokens on your military card, you can spend one or both to add a bonus to your roll. Caravans can also garner you another player’s Diplomacy card, which has certain benefits dependent on the card.
4) Placing a control tokens mean you’ve claimed territory (that particular space), which is necessary for collecting trade tokens (a “mature” city garners you a set number of trade tokens once you’ve “controlled” all adjacent tiles), collecting resources such as marble or diamonds, or for building cities (your build cities a certain number of spaces from a space you’ve controlled with a token).
5) The terrain has an impact on your choices. In order of scaled “easiness”, the terrains are 1-grasslands, 2-hills, 3-forest, 4-desert, and 5-mountains. To travel through a desert is considered difficult, so that 4 means your Economy card (the one that moves your caravan) needs to be in the 4 or 5 slot. Similary, to build a city in a mountain space means your Industry card has to be in the 5 slot.

There are more rules and factors that come into play, but that’s the general gist. As noted at the start, I’d say the learning curve is relatively steep the first time ( a lot of going back to the instruction booklet), but past the first game or two, it comes pretty easily. I’ve certainly played games with a far steeper curve and one that takes longer to get to know game play well. If I were ranking learning curves on a ten-point scale, I’d probably put this around a 6.

Turns move slowly the first time or two as people try to remember what they can do, what they need to do, etc. But after the first hour each player moves pretty quickly through their turns as you’ve gotten used to how to deal with the complexities of those shifting slots under the Focus bar. As people get closer to each other, things slow again as players try and figure out cost-benefit of attacking, but then as before, after a few attacks those move quickly.

I liked the game quite a bit. More than my two family members, but I tend to have more patience for the slowness of things and I mind long game less than they do. They did like it enough to play again. And as mentioned, I like that you can self-adjust your length simply by cutting out one of the agendas. It’s a game we’ll definitely keep and keep playing.
text_fidelity_b: Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games

text_fidelity_a:
DC Superheroes Top Trumps Match Board Game This is a fun game. My boyfriend and I played it. It is only a two-player match game like tic-tac-toe or battleship. The youngest player starts and both players get two cards which they keep face down until the end of the game. The first player pushes out a cube in the top left corner of the game grid. The next player then pushes out another cube on the board with that same cube. The play continues with each player pushing out the next cube with the previous cube just played without using the same grid hole. The idea is to match five of the same characters in a row either horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. When one player indicates a match, the losing player turns over their cards and if the character on one of the cards matches the winning players match, then that person now wins the game. If there is no match, then the winner keeps his win.

The game is simple, yet fun, and is full of strategy. There are two negatives, however. The game case is difficult to open and it feels like I am going to break off the plastic prongs when I pull it apart. Also, the game wobbles a bit when the outside "wings" are down. Third, it is easy to knock all the cubes out of the game grid. As my boyfriend was playing, he titled the game just a bit to see the characters better and many of the cubes fell out. Other than the lackluster quality of the game parts, the game itself is wonderfully simple and tremendous fun.
text_fidelity_b: DC Superheroes Top Trumps Match Board Game

The Wolves Board Game | Wolf Themed Survival Strategy Game | Highly Interactive Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 14+ | 2-5 Players | Avg. Playtime 75 Minutes | Made by Pandasaurus Games I'm a wolf lover as well as a game nerd and couldn't pass this one up! It is absolutely beautiful out of the box. I'm impressed they kept it to a $50 price point with the level of detail here, I've seen similar games priced closer to $80!

I haven't had a chance to play yet because I need to get folks together but I did watch a video playthrough about the rules after reading the guide so that I'd be prepared. They are complex but once I watched the video it made a lot more sense. It's definitely tactic-heavy in that you need to change strategy based on what your opponent is doing or what phase of the moon it is on. I love many of the creative points in the design, and I love a game with a very clear endpoint because I hate games that go on forever! 75 minutes is perfect for a game night.

I especially love the design of the wolf cards. They are extremely clear where the tiles and meeples go etc. It's not only attractive but it also includes reminder text which is really helpful for absent-minded players like myself. I love how the rules for your items level up as you get more pieces on the board.

My favorite part about games like this is that it's possible to lose a battle here and there and not feel discouraged halfway through. Since a lot of scoring can happen later, it keeps players invested until the end. This generation of games is so different from the ones before!

My only complaint is that with a game like this it is so easy to lose a meeple because they are so small and so many. This can make it hard to trust strangers with at board-game meetups.
text_fidelity_b: The Wolves Board Game | Wolf Themed Survival Strategy Game | Highly Interactive Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 14+ | 2-5 Players | Avg. Playtime 75 Minutes | Made by Pandasaurus Games

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope Imperial Star Destroyer 75252 Building Kit (4,784 Pieces) The first thing I noticed about this set was the weight. This is the first LEGO set that I've gotten that I would actually describe as heavy. That's a lot of brick. The box is nice, and contains several smaller boxes. Those boxes have some blueprint art on them, but no useful labeling as to where to begin. You need to open them all anyway, because the unlabeled bags of large parts are mixed in with some of the later bags, despite being needed early on. The bag numbering only goes up to about 20, but there are many bags for each number and the bags have bags in them. The instruction book is huge and spiral bound, with some nice history in the early pages.

The set goes together surprisingly quickly early on, starting with the display base and docking clamps, which the ship is built on, with sections being build and then clipped on. The internal support structure is well engineered and solid. You get a good impression of the overall size and shape of the ship by the time you are done with bag 2.

At first glance, this may look like a tedious grey set where all the parts look the same, but the insides are brightly colored. This is really nice because the parts being built are often rotated between panels, and the colors really help with both finding the parts and orienting with the instructions. When you're done, it also makes it easy to spot anything you missed, because the grey exterior will have rainbow colors there.

One disappointment is the thin area down the sides of the ship. I like them fine individually, but the instructions have you build them identically, so rather than being bilaterally symmetrical, one side looks like it's upside down compared to the other. I understand this saved them some pages, and made construction a little easier, but I would've appreciated a heads up so I could build it mirrored, since I think that would've worked out fine, at least for the greebles on the outside. I may actually take one side apart and redo it, though It's the kind of detail that an observer might not notice because this thing is so big. There are other areas that are more obviously asymmetrical, which is true to the movie, but looks really jarring to me the way they implemented it.

After completing it, I feel like it was designed by two different teams of people. The interior structure is an awesome feat of engineering, and so sturdy you can carry the whole thing by an interior handle, despite its great weight, and they did it with all existing parts. The exterior is about as expected in a Lego set. The transition between the two is weak. Brushing against it risks knocking things off. Sometimes it's just some barely attached pieces on the back, other times something obviously comes apart inside that's going to take some doing to get to and fix. The different sections are often just resting loosely on each other and sometimes look uneven. There is a tiny and comically inadequate clip to hold the four sections of the front in alignment. You may want to think about what you're going to do with it when it's done. It's large, heavy, and oddly shaped. Comes on a nice stand though.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope Imperial Star Destroyer 75252 Building Kit (4,784 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
Mini Human Skeleton Model for Anatomy, 17.7'' Full Body Human Skeleton Model with Movable Arms and Legs on Plastic Base for Medical Teaching Learning, Kids Learning Education Display Tool Gift Wow, is this a toy? Because it is full of problems and inaccuracies. I’d like to start with my side-by-side photo showing some of the most egregious problems.
On the right hand with a black background is how it is supposed to look, and on the left is how it actually looks.
*Spinal alignment: any human with this type of alignment has a serious medical condition. The spine is supposed to have curvature in order to support the weight properly. As you can see by the Sideview of this toy, there is minimal curvature, and what little there is would lead the person to fall backwards. This is particularly problematic along the cervical and lumbar vertebrae (neck and lower back)
*The ribcage on this silly toy flares out at the bottom in a bizzarre way that doesn’t represent normal anatomy. Likewise, there is no attempt to indicate where the bone ends and the cartilaginous attachment points begin. Our ribs are not solid bone all the way from the vertebral column to the sternum. There’s supposed to be cartilage toward the midline as the ribs approach the sternum. Even if this model can’t indicate that, there should at least have been some sort of scoring or line or something.
The radius and ulna are ridiculous. Their thickness and size are not in correct proportion with the rest of the body. Also, why is this not in anatomical position?
Then there’s the attachment from the humerus to the glenoid fossa of the scapula, which cannot be seen in the poster or in this model. That’s just not how our arms are attached at all. Like the hip joint, the shoulder is a ball and socket joint, albeit a much shallower one than the hips. The way this is attached is so misleading and terrible. I can’t even deal with it. And circling back once again to the alignment of the spine, the pelvic bowl is completely wrong. It’s supposed to tilt downward much more.
So basically this is garbage. It’s not good for art, and it’s not really good for teaching either. What a shame. It did have some things going for it, but the issues I pointed out are too significant to ignore.

Hot Wheels 20-Pack of 1:64 Scale Toy Sports & Race Cars, Collectible Vehicles (Styles May Vary) It might seem as if 20 cars is too much at once. Nope! It is wonderful.

Days as a five year-old were best filled with playing in complete abandon. The freedom proffered by youth needed only a few toys to complete the ever-present joy. A few toys which mattered included several tattered but friendly books, a truck or two, an odd shovel and bucket, and, the coup de grace, a Hot Wheels car. Mattel makes a track as well, but a well-made car could take a boy places. This set of 20 is what kindergartners drool over.

A boy has everything in this set: vehicles of all colors, a few truck varieties, some funny looking cars. There are plenty, and frankly, since a few will invariably wind up lost under the couch, eaten by the dog, and buried with other treasures in the garden, having 20 quickly becomes justified.

Why a Hot Wheels car? Because they are made with hard steel. They are painted with a slick color. They hold up to frequent tastings, sand grindings, dirt smearings and other nonsense that comes with power racing in a sandbox. Sticky chocolate wipes off with warm water, and grime comes out with a good spray under the faucet.

The wheels themselves have a bounce peculiar to a genuine Hot Wheels vehicle. That's how my brother and I made sure it had adequate fuel. Ten bounces should be enough, we figured, and usually, we were right.

I fully recommend the "Hot Wheels 20-Car Gift Pack."

Anthony Trendl
AmericanSpeechwriter.com

text_fidelity_a:
Escape Room in a Box: Flashback, Escape Room Game with 19 Puzzles and 4 Locks, Can Pair with Amazon Alexa, For Adults and Teens 13 Years Old and Up It's an 80s themed box, with a name like "Flashback" that has nothing to do with the 80s, and very little to do with "flashbacks". It's actually about werewolves, a magic ring, and bad poetry. The story makes no sense at all, and that's the easiest element of an escape room, really. Fortunately, everything else in this box is pretty good.

We played with a group of 4 people, which was perfect. You could even do six and have a great time with it. The game is broken into three paths - red, purple and blue, each with a very vague theme like "poems" (blue), "childhood" (purple) and "dinosaurs" (red) - and you need to complete all three in order to win. We broke our group of four into two teams of two and tackled blue and purple envelopes separately, then worked together on the red and the final puzzle. Each envelope took us roughly the same amount of time to beat, and the final puzzle was appropriately paced to be solved quickly. Most other escape room games we've played, from Unlock to Exit to Escape the Room all suffer from pacing problems, or narrowing you down to having only one puzzle or a few cards to work with at one time, which is nice for pointing out the way to solve some more complex puzzles, but which makes it rather difficult to play with more than two people - this box has solved that problem.

Overall, we were pretty impressed with this with a few caveats. One of the puzzles requires you to do something to the game pieces that is spelled out early on in the letter. It wasn't difficult to figure out what to do, but it was difficult to execute. It's hard to say more without giving out spoilers for one of the "coolest" puzzles in the box, but let's just say that it was mechanically difficult to work with. One of the puzzles at the end of the game required another outside prop that's easy to deal with, but the amount of finagleing with the pieces and the prop left us questioning if we had solved that puzzle correctly (we did, but it wasn't quite clear).

One touch that I particularly liked was how the game color-coded everything according to the paths/envelopes, and how the locked boxes worked - they performed exacly as they should have, and they were high enough quality that we felt like we could toss them around a little without any issues.

This is expensive for a one-time-use product, but it's definitely my favorite of the escape room games for a medium to large sized group, and it's probably pretty good for two slueths to solve on their own as well.

Solved in 1:07:11.
text_fidelity_b: Escape Room in a Box: Flashback, Escape Room Game with 19 Puzzles and 4 Locks, Can Pair with Amazon Alexa, For Adults and Teens 13 Years Old and Up

Both sides of each pentagon piece are faceted, so they have texture instead of being smooth. The facets make the sphere very sparkly, even in a dimly lit room.

The magnets are strong and hold securely. The pieces snap together with very loud clicks, so this might not be the best fidget if you need to be quiet while using it. But if noise isn’t a problem, this is a very satisfying fidget. I like to build and crumple the sphere, or simply stack the pentagons.

I noticed a few sharp bits of plastic, mainly around the openings for the magnets. I didn’t feel any sharp bits on the surfaces of the pentagons.

Electric Wiggle Car Ride On Toy, ANPABO 2 in 1 Wiggle Car with Rechargeable Battery and Pedal, Anti-Rollover Wheels with Colorful Lights, Swing Car for Toddlers and Kids Age 3 Years up Update: after a few months of off/on use- ours figured out how to ride on his own… don’t give up- kids can get the hang of it just fine!!!

Super excited in theory.. with ability to use manually or with electronic option as needed- it seemed ideal by just a flip of a switch on bottom. Only for some reason, pedal doesn’t respond every time like it should!! (Yes! battery is full when trying it- yet 15% of time it wont respond electronically- reason deducted x1 star!!?) When pedal engages- scooter is stable, easy to glide and maneuver.. and enjoyed. Battery outlasts our toddler whose rides for 15-25min straight and it hasn’t run out! (For reference: our little is 33mo, 36lb, 38” tall.. almost 3yr old.)

because of electronic component- ours struggles to grasp concept without using the pedal since he’s learned to ride with the electronic aid! So, when it fails to respond or we have pedal off- he just “jerks” scooter back/forth and side/side- its as if he’s trying to get it to do what it “should..” by tugging it into motion. For some reason.. he doesn’t naturally get moving scooter without electronic help so, it can leaves him fristrated.

Instructions are straightforward and connecting handle atop the scooter can be a tad tricky and tight.. Best if use included hardware to connect all screws loosely first THEN, tighten after all parts are aligned. Light up wheels are just extra!!! Not needed and not sure how long they’ll last esp. rider encountered water elements? I love the “long press” music feature- ha, it’s my fav. **bc, It shuts music all the way off!!

We’ve only used inside on tile and large smooth nape rug. No tire markings is nice.. I like inside option bc it’s winter here! I realize some issues had may be caused by our rider himself- but feel pedal should not be a problem we have to deal with if it’s charged. Hoping info can help decision.. stay safe everyone!
